title: Soap and Candles
premise: Survey from Wolf Point what Daniel Elston and Company's works up the North Branch manufactured, compose a concise list on South Water Street, determine what to carry, and convey it home to a boarding house behind Peck's store.

opening.text:
JAUNT: SOAP AND CANDLES. Dusk arrives progressively earlier, because autumn signals that the prolonged darkness is approaching: once the lake freezes, "during the long six months of winter the inhabitants, were cut off from the rest of the world". Illumination and soap are what sustain a crowded boarding house through those isolated months.

You board in the log house behind Peck's store. Survey the North Branch toward the soap and candle works, compose a concise list on South Water Street, determine what to carry, and convey it home before complete darkness descends.

stops.text: Commence at Wolf Point and survey the North Branch to its eastern bank, where the scene positions Daniel Elston and Company's works, although no source establishes the actual location. Their notice, printed during 1833 and 1834, advertised hard and soft soap, wax and other candles, and offered cash for tallow and household ashes. Every family's kitchen fat and fireplace ashes return transformed into soap and illumination.

choices.label: Light for the evenings matters most
choices.consequence: Candles are positioned prominently at the top of the household list.

choices.label: Soap for washing day matters most
choices.consequence: Soap is positioned prominently at the top of the household list.

stops.narrative: Tallow and ashes enter the works, while soap and illumination emerge for the town.

stops.text: Across the river to Jones's grocery on South Water Street. His November 1833 notice advertised sugar and most varieties of provisions at the lowest prices, although whether he stocked soap or candles it does not specify, and only the street itself constitutes evidence. Candles mean fire, and the town comprehends the hazard: since 1833 every stovepipe penetrating a roof must be "guarded by tin or sheet iron".

choices.label: Carry candles home
choices.consequence: A bundle of candles, individually dipped in tallow and secured together with string.

choices.label: Carry a cake of hard soap
choices.consequence: One substantial cake of hard soap, practically as weighty as a building brick.

choices.label: Carry some of each
choices.consequence: A considerably heavier armful, encompassing the entire list.

stops.narrative: Compose the list methodically, and determine what you will carry home.

stops.text: Proceed to Lake Street and the two-story frame store Thomas Church constructed, reputedly the first store building on the street. Church arrived in 1834, the year business "began to extend to Lake street". A single undated sentence constitutes the entirety of the evidence, and because it identifies no merchandise, nothing is purchased here.
stops.narrative: Redistribute the bundle in your arms and inventory what you are carrying.

stops.text: Return to the log house behind Peck's store, which Andreas identifies as Mrs Rufus Brown's, one of the first-class boarding houses. In 1834, he writes, such establishments were perpetually full, occasionally accommodating three in a bed. Nevertheless, Moses and Kirkland maintain the snowbound months were "perhaps, the most enjoyable of the entire year".
stops.narrative: A solitary candle illuminates a considerable amount in a crowded room.

legs.note: Over the South Branch by a bridge and east to South Water Street.
legs.story: With the priority between soap and illumination determined, the list follows.

legs.note: A block south to Lake Street.
Back toward the rear of Peck's corner at South Water and LaSalle.
legs.story: The concluding steps homeward with the bundle balanced in your arms.

endings.text: Soap and candles both, conveyed home to the log house behind Peck's, so the entire list is complete, whichever item occupied the top position. Let the interminable winter arrive.
Candles at the top of the list, and candles conveyed home, so tonight the crowded room behind Peck's possesses illumination for reading and mending, and the darkness arrives somewhat later.
With soap prioritized at the top of the list and successfully conveyed home, the accumulated laundry need wait no longer.
You departed intending to purchase one item and conveyed home the alternative, which will be required soon enough, and the list will endure until next time.

keepsake.title: Light for the Evening
keepsake.text: A fictional note documenting a concise list and what you carried home from it in July 1835. No authentic sale, price or customer of any shop is recorded on it.

evidence.text: B. Jones's 'Grocery & Provision Store' advertisement in the first number of the Chicago Democrat says he keeps constantly on hand sugar and most kinds of provisions, for sale at the lowest prices. It gives no street, and a damaged line between may have named more goods.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 5, the advertisement headed 'Grocery & Provision Store. B. JONES.' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c018). Transcription-mediated reading of a damaged scan.

evidence.text: Jones's store is placed on the south side of South Water Street just east of Wells; the street is the evidence and the block is not.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas lists Jones among the South Water Street district's advertisers; neither he nor the advertisement gives a block, so the structure record grades the coordinate reconstructed and the stop calls the block our placement. The two sources disagree on the initial (B. or H.), so the stop says only Jones.

evidence.text: Daniel Elston & Co.'s 'Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory' advertisement announces that they have commenced the manufacture of soap and candles, keep an assortment of hard and soft soap, wax and other candles, and pay cash for tallow in any quantity and for good house ashes.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 6, the advertisement headed 'Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c030); the partner's name is lost under a tear in the scan. Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The same Elston & Co. advertisement was still printed in the Chicago Democrat of 2 July 1834.
evidence.locator: 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 1 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_02#c007). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: No source gives the works' site: the advertisement and Andreas's summary of it name the firm and the trade and no street. The scene places it on the east bank of the North Branch above the forks.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record's position is a conjectural proposal that cites no source for the site; the stop therefore says the place is ours and stays an exterior observation from the road. Nothing records a shop counter at the works.

evidence.text: The first stop is the scene's typed viewpoint 'The forks, from Wolf Point', on the west bank where the North and South Branches meet; the works as the scene places it stands about 230 m up the North Branch, on the far bank. The viewpoint is a camera position, not a claimed path or a place anyone stood.
evidence.reasoning: DRLOIH puts Wolf Point on the west bank at the forks. The anchor stands at local E -100, N -28 in data/scenes/1835.json and elston_soap_candle_manufactory's placement at E -13, N +184, so the works is looked at across the water, as the stop says, and its site stays the scene's conjecture (elston-place).

evidence.text: Tallow and house ashes are the two inputs of soap making, the ashes leached for lye and boiled with rendered tallow; candles are the same tallow moulded or dipped.
evidence.reasoning: The advertisement states what the firm bought (tallow, house ashes) and what it sold (soap, candles); the process that joins them is the ordinary one and is the structure record's own inference about the plant, not a description of these works.

evidence.text: An uncredited modern note says the first store building on Lake Street, a two-storey frame structure, was built by Thomas Church. It gives no year, no stock and no address, and this project grades the note as its weakest kind of source.
evidence.locator: Chicagology, early street maps gallery, the editorial addendum at the foot of the page: the Thomas Church sentence (accessed 2026-08-11).

evidence.text: Church's store is placed mid-block on the north side of Lake Street between LaSalle and Clark; the street is attested and the block is not.
evidence.reasoning: The note says 'Lake Street' only. The structure record chose an unclaimed stretch and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop claims no front door and nothing sold.

evidence.text: Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as keeper of one of the first-class boarding houses, and places Brown's log house as the first building in the rear of Peck's store.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 132, boarding-house paragraph; p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography.

evidence.text: With no railroads, canals or telegraphs, 'during the long six months of winter the inhabitants, were cut off from the rest of the world'. 'There was nothing coming in, and there was no means of sending anything out of the town. And yet these winter months were, perhaps, the most enjoyable of the entire year.'
evidence.locator: p. 99, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13364-13371 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The trustees' first ordinance, of 6 November 1833, 'prohibited the passing of stove-pipes through the roof, partition or side of any building, unless guarded by tin or sheet iron, under penalty of $5'.
evidence.locator: p. 93, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12641-12646 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1834 'Business, which had heretofore been confined to South Water street on the South Side, began to extend to Lake street'; Thomas Church is among that year's arrivals who became leading citizens.
evidence.locator: p. 95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12802-12821 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The boarding house is placed directly behind Peck's store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle; its distance behind the store is not documented.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the position only relative to Peck's store. The structure record sets the house directly south of the store's footprint on the same lot line and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop calls the exact spot our placement.

evidence.text: Andreas says the town's hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'.
evidence.reasoning: The sentence describes the houses of 1834 as a class, as the structure record and household file quote it; the stop carries it a year forward to one house of that class in a town the June 1835 papers also found crowded, and says 1834.

evidence.text: The boarder, the list, which item stands at the top of it, the route, the bundle carried home, where it was obtained, the endings, the timing inputs and the Light for the Evening keepsake are invented connective narrative. No sale, price or customer of any shop is documented, and no named person is met.
